CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Pursue a negotiated truce at the G20 dinner with Trump. Offer a credible package of purchase commitments and incremental market-opening measures sufficient to forestall the January 1 escalation to 25% tariffs, but make no structural concessions on industrial policy or Made in China 2025. The goal is to buy 6-12 months of tariff stability while domestic stimulus takes hold.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE:

Threat reading (0.45 — elevated but not existential): The trade war has already imposed material costs on China. Tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese exports to the US (List 1+2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%), and Trump has threatened to extend to all $500B+ and raise List 3 to 25% on January 1 (timeline: Sep 17, Sep 24 entries). China's GDP growth slowed to 6.5% in Q3, the weakest since Q1 2009, missing expectations (CNBC, Oct 19). The Shanghai Composite has fallen ~30% year-to-date, among the world's worst performers alongside Turkey and Argentina (Reuters, Sep 12). The yuan has depreciated ~6% against the dollar (CNN, Oct 8). Consumer confidence is falling — auto sales dropped 11.7% YoY in October, smartphone shipments fell 15.2% in Q3, and Golden Week consumer spending grew at the slowest pace since 2000 (SCMP, Nov 23). However, this is not yet existential: 6.5% growth is still above target, exports held up at 11% growth in October partly due to front-loading, and Beijing has room for further RRR cuts and fiscal stimulus. The threat is serious and accelerating, but China retains policy buffers.

Action stance (-0.05 — lean toward negotiation): Several factors counsel restraint rather than retaliation or escalation. First, China's retaliation capacity is nearly exhausted — it has already tariffed ~$110B of US imports but cannot match dollar-for-dollar given the $506B vs $130B trade asymmetry (Business Insider, Nov 9). Second, the soybean tariff is backfiring domestically: China cut US soybean imports 80%+ in September but faces supply shortfalls and rising food prices, as Brazil cannot fully replace US supply (CNN, Oct 1; farmpolicynews, Nov 6). Third, Trump himself is showing cracks — the NYT (Nov 28) reports 'creeping anxiety' about market costs, GM layoffs, and rising rates, with moderates like Kudlow and Mnuchin pushing for a deal. The cancellation of preparatory talks and APEC's failure to produce a joint communique (CNN, Nov 19) signal that both sides are posturing, but Trump's willingness to meet over dinner suggests he wants an off-ramp. China should offer enough — purchase commitments, perhaps a broad tariff reduction on all imports — to give Trump a headline win, while preserving its industrial policy autonomy. Escalation would risk the full $500B+ tariff extension and potential entity-list actions against firms like Huawei, which would be far more damaging. The strategic patience approach — concede purchases, protect technology policy — is the correct play.
